AI in This Course

AI is a cutting-edge research technology, and I want you to be using cutting-edge research technologies. So the question in this course is not whether AI is good or bad. The question is how to use it well, and when not to use it at all.

Principles

Responsibility

Maybe you wrote something entirely yourself. More likely a co-author, an editor, or an assistant (human or machine) had a hand in it: whether hidden or open, authorship is always a collective enterprise. Either way, when you submit something, in this class or anywhere else in life, you are taking responsibility for it: for its claims, its evidence, and its mistakes.

You Have Touched Every Word

Does that mean there was zero AI involved? No. AI drives spellcheckers and grammar checkers, internet searches and e-readers: these are good tools and you should be using them. It means that you have read, considered, and stand behind every single word of what you submit.

AI Can Help You Think, but the Claims and Evidence Must Be Yours

Use AI to test ideas, find gaps, and push back on your reasoning. But the claims you make, and the evidence you use to support them, must be your own, and you must have verified them.

How These Principles Apply to the Instructor

I hold myself to the same standards.

  • Course content: I will not use AI to draft the prose in course content. Every word that I present to you, in writing or in audio, comes from me. Even when the voice you hear in a recording is AI-generated, the script behind it is mine.
  • Grading: I will never, ever use AI for grading. Not as a first pass, not as a suggestion, not at all.
  • Your work: I will never put student work into any tool, AI or otherwise, that Pitt has not approved for use with University data.

  • Where I do use AI: to produce engaging lecture videos and clear audio; to design websites like the one you are reading now; and constantly, in my own research and work. AI as an editorial and exploratory aid, never as the source of claims or historical evidence.

How These Principles Apply to Students

I design my courses to harness AI in some places and to take it out of the equation in others, depending on the purpose of each exercise. (Pitt’s Teaching Center describes a range of approaches to generative AI in courses; this course uses several of them, assignment by assignment.) The upshot: if you can (or cannot) use AI on something, that is by design.

That is why you will see a lot of “old-fashioned” exercises in this course, many of them handwritten. That is not an aversion to AI. These exercises are valuable in their own right, and some of them will make you better at using AI: learning to tell good AI-produced prose from bad, and finding your own voice and your own standards, so that you can then use AI to help you meet them.

A quite reasonable reaction to hand-written, in-class assignments might well be: “I will never have to do this in Real Life, why on earth are we being tormented this way?” The invention of the calculator rendered long division obsolete… and yet you still memorize multiplication tables and carry out those decimals by hand in grade school. The calculator changed the purpose of those activities, making them mostly a means to the end of learning mathematical reasoning rather than an end in themselves. Writing is no different: if you want to tell AI what is good writing, rather than the other way around, you need to spend some alone time with pen, paper, and your own intellect.

AI as a Study Aid

AI can be an excellent aid while you prepare for class, depending on how you use it. For example:

  • Self-quizzing on readings and recorded lectures before class
  • Background and context: who is this person, where is this place, what does this term mean?
  • Summaries and literature reviews to orient yourself before (not instead of) a close reading
  • Devil’s advocate, or “Reviewer 2”: ask AI to attack your reading of a primary source, then decide whether the criticism holds up
  • Untangling a difficult passage, then checking the explanation against the source itself

In every case, the principles above still apply: you are responsible for the content and the analysis. Pitt’s own standard for AI use makes the same point: you are accountable for anything you produce with AI, and for verifying its accuracy.

Assignments

Any assignment that involves AI can be completed with the tools Pitt provides to students. No paid subscription is ever required.

The Alternative Grading Option has its own, stricter rule: no AI at all.
